results.name: set_range_yes_correlation
results.description: Pearson correlation, across multi-example sets with >=10 trials, between the examples' numeric range (max-min) and the set's yes rate on non-example targets; observed above null means people broaden generalization with set spread more than the model (spread matters more), below means less.
results.code:
# name: set_range_yes_correlation
# description: Pearson correlation, across multi-example sets with >=10 trials, between the examples' numeric range (max-min) and the set's yes rate on non-example targets; observed above null means people broaden generalization with set spread more than the model (spread matters more), below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    present = ~np.isnan(E)
    Ei = np.where(present, E, 0).astype(int)
    def dmask(a):
        m = (1 << (a % 10)) | np.where(a >= 10, 1 << ((a // 10) % 10), 0) | np.where(a >= 100, 2, 0)
        return np.where(a > 0, m, 0)
    EM = dmask(Ei)
    union = np.bitwise_or.reduce(EM, axis=1)
    inter = np.bitwise_and.reduce(np.where(present, EM, 1023), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    TM = dmask(t)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n_ex = present.sum(axis=1)
    is_ex = (Ei == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    rng = np.where(present, Ei, -1).max(axis=1) - np.where(present, Ei, 999).min(axis=1)
    m = (n_ex >= 2) & ~is_ex
    g = pd.DataFrame({"s": df["number_set"].to_numpy()[m], "rng": rng[m], "r": r[m]}).groupby("s").agg(rng=("rng", "first"), y=("r", "mean"), n=("r", "size"))
    g = g[g["n"] >= 10]
    if len(g) < 3 or g["y"].std() == 0 or g["rng"].std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(g["rng"], g["y"])[0, 1])

results.name: warmup_yes_difference
results.description: Yes rate on early trials (trial_index < 50) minus yes rate on all later trials; observed above null means people say yes more at the start of the session (a warm-up / calibration effect the stationary model cannot produce), below means they start more conservative.

    Ei = np.where(present, E, 0).astype(int)

        return np.where(a > 0, m, 0)
    EM = dmask(Ei)
    union = np.bitwise_or.reduce(EM, axis=1)
    inter = np.bitwise_and.reduce(np.where(present, EM, 1023), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    TM = dmask(t)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()

results.name: first_vs_last_example_digit_share
results.description: In multi-example sets, among non-example targets, yes rate for targets sharing a digit with the last-shown example but not the first minus yes rate for targets sharing a digit with the first-shown example but not the last; the model is order-invariant, so observed above null means recency in digit-based generalization, below means primacy.
results.code:
# name: first_vs_last_example_digit_share
# description: In multi-example sets, among non-example targets, yes rate for targets sharing a digit with the last-shown example but not the first minus yes rate for targets sharing a digit with the first-shown example but not the last; the model is order-invariant, so observed above null means recency in digit-based generalization, below means primacy.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    present = ~np.isnan(E)
    Ei = np.where(present, E, 0).astype(int)
    def dmask(a):
        m = (1 << (a % 10)) | np.where(a >= 10, 1 << ((a // 10) % 10), 0) | np.where(a >= 100, 2, 0)
        return np.where(a > 0, m, 0)
    EM = dmask(Ei)
    union = np.bitwise_or.reduce(EM, axis=1)
    inter = np.bitwise_and.reduce(np.where(present, EM, 1023), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    TM = dmask(t)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n_ex = present.sum(axis=1)
    is_ex = (Ei == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    first = EM[:, 0]
    last_idx = n_ex - 1
    last = EM[np.arange(len(EM)), last_idx]
    m = (n_ex >= 2) & ~is_ex
    sl = (TM & last) > 0
    sf = (TM & first) > 0
    return rate(m & sl & ~sf) - rate(m & sf & ~sl)

results.name: small_vs_large_unrelated_target
results.description: Among non-example targets sharing no digit with any example and more than 15 from every example, yes rate for targets <=30 minus targets >=70; observed above null means people favour small numbers a priori (a magnitude bias the model lacks), below means they favour large numbers more than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: small_vs_large_unrelated_target
# description: Among non-example targets sharing no digit with any example and more than 15 from every example, yes rate for targets <=30 minus targets >=70; observed above null means people favour small numbers a priori (a magnitude bias the model lacks), below means they favour large numbers more than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    present = ~np.isnan(E)
    Ei = np.where(present, E, 0).astype(int)
    def dmask(a):
        m = (1 << (a % 10)) | np.where(a >= 10, 1 << ((a // 10) % 10), 0) | np.where(a >= 100, 2, 0)
        return np.where(a > 0, m, 0)
    EM = dmask(Ei)
    union = np.bitwise_or.reduce(EM, axis=1)
    inter = np.bitwise_and.reduce(np.where(present, EM, 1023), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    TM = dmask(t)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n_ex = present.sum(axis=1)
    is_ex = (Ei == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    dist = np.where(present, np.abs(Ei - t[:, None]), 999).min(axis=1)
    base = ~is_ex & ((TM & union) == 0) & (dist > 15)
    return rate(base & (t <= 30)) - rate(base & (t >= 70))

results.name: common_digit_multi_example_contrast
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that all contain a common digit, yes rate for non-example targets containing a common digit minus yes rate for non-example targets containing none of the examples' digits; observed above null means the model under-produces contains-digit generalization from multiple examples (rule posterior too diffuse), below means it over-produces it.

# name: common_digit_multi_example_contrast
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that all contain a common digit, yes rate for non-example targets containing a common digit minus yes rate for non-example targets containing none of the examples' digits; observed above null means the model under-produces contains-digit generalization from multiple examples (rule posterior too diffuse), below means it over-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    present = ~np.isnan(E)
    Ei = np.where(present, E, 0).astype(int)
    def dmask(a):
        m = (1 << (a % 10)) | np.where(a >= 10, 1 << ((a // 10) % 10), 0) | np.where(a >= 100, 2, 0)
        return np.where(a > 0, m, 0)
    EM = dmask(Ei)
    union = np.bitwise_or.reduce(EM, axis=1)
    inter = np.bitwise_and.reduce(np.where(present, EM, 1023), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    TM = dmask(t)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n_ex = present.sum(axis=1)
    is_ex = (Ei == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    base = (n_ex >= 2) & (inter > 0) & ~is_ex
    return rate(base & ((TM & inter) > 0)) - rate(base & ((TM & union) == 0))

results.name: round_number_target_bonus

        return np.where(a > 0, m, 0)

    inter = np.bitwise_and.reduce(np.where(present, EM, 1023), axis=1)

results.name: single_example_magnitude_neighbourhood
results.description: For one-example sets, among targets sharing no digit with the example, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example minus targets more than 30 away; observed above null means people generalize from a single number by magnitude similarity more than the model's interval hypotheses (outcompeted by digit rules) allow, below means less.

# name: single_example_magnitude_neighbourhood
# description: For one-example sets, among targets sharing no digit with the example, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example minus targets more than 30 away; observed above null means people generalize from a single number by magnitude similarity more than the model's interval hypotheses (outcompeted by digit rules) allow, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    present = ~np.isnan(E)
    Ei = np.where(present, E, 0).astype(int)
    def dmask(a):
        m = (1 << (a % 10)) | np.where(a >= 10, 1 << ((a // 10) % 10), 0) | np.where(a >= 100, 2, 0)
        return np.where(a > 0, m, 0)
    EM = dmask(Ei)
    union = np.bitwise_or.reduce(EM, axis=1)
    inter = np.bitwise_and.reduce(np.where(present, EM, 1023), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    TM = dmask(t)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()

    is_ex = (Ei == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    m = (n_ex == 1) & ~is_ex & ((TM & union) == 0)

    return rate(m & (dist <= 10)) - rate(m & (dist > 30))

results.name: two_digit_overlap_contrast
results.description: Among non-example two-digit targets 10-99 with two distinct digits, yes rate when both of the target's digits occur among the examples' digits minus yes rate when exactly one does; observed above null means people reward multiple digit overlap (e.g. digit reversals like 38/83) more than the model's sum of single contains-digit rules, below means less.
results.code:
# name: two_digit_overlap_contrast
# description: Among non-example two-digit targets 10-99 with two distinct digits, yes rate when both of the target's digits occur among the examples' digits minus yes rate when exactly one does; observed above null means people reward multiple digit overlap (e.g. digit reversals like 38/83) more than the model's sum of single contains-digit rules, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    present = ~np.isnan(E)
    Ei = np.where(present, E, 0).astype(int)
    def dmask(a):
        m = (1 << (a % 10)) | np.where(a >= 10, 1 << ((a // 10) % 10), 0) | np.where(a >= 100, 2, 0)
        return np.where(a > 0, m, 0)
    EM = dmask(Ei)
    union = np.bitwise_or.reduce(EM, axis=1)
    inter = np.bitwise_and.reduce(np.where(present, EM, 1023), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    TM = dmask(t)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n_ex = present.sum(axis=1)
    is_ex = (Ei == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    two = (t >= 10) & (t <= 99) & ((t // 10) != (t % 10)) & ~is_ex
    tens_in = ((union >> (t // 10)) & 1) == 1
    units_in = ((union >> (t % 10)) & 1) == 1
    return rate(two & tens_in & units_in) - rate(two & (tens_in ^ units_in))
